newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Smuggling booms as Colombian peso strengthens.
newsitem.headline: Smuggling booms as Colombian peso strengthens.

text.p: Smuggling foreign goods into Colombia has boomed on the back of the strengthening peso and could hamper economic recovery in the first half of 1997, an influential financial group said on Sunday.

In its weekly report, the National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) said contraband had been on the rise since August and forecast it would continue to undermine legitimate business operations for the next six months.

As the peso has strengthened against the U.S. dollar, smugglers have seen their profit margins grow since the value of domestically-produced products has risen while that of foreign-made items was falling in peso terms.
"Since last year many businessmen stopped highlighting contraband goods as a major problem. But the issue is once again growing in importance since August," the ANIF report said.

"The worst thing is that the full effect of the revaluation of the peso on illegal imports takes up to six months to filter through. That fact will hamper the recovery of important sectors of the economy in the first half of 1997," it added.

The ANIF report said the strong peso was the prime cause for increased smuggling, given that the fragile state of the economy -- expected to register one of its lowest growth rates in a decade in 1996 -- had failed to fuel a rise in demand.

At close of trade on Friday, the peso stood at 995.25 to the U.S. dollar. It has lost less than three percent of its value since the start of the year, despite government targets of a 13.5 percent devaluation of the peso during 1996.
The strong peso has brought sharp recriminations against the government and the central bank from key export sectors, which have seen the peso value of exports fall.
